## Scientist, engineer, and model builder

I am a Brazilian biomedical engineer and computational scientist with a
PhD in Biomedical Engineering from Johns Hopkins University. I am currently
a postdoctoral fellow at the Popel Systems Biology Lab (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine),
where I develop mechanistic models to support translational research and
drug development.

My work lies at the intersection of biology, pharmacology, and computation.
I use mathematical models to organize complex biological knowledge, test
mechanistic hypotheses, quantify uncertainty, identify biomarkers and investigate how differences
between individuals may influence treatment response.

## My research path

My research began in mechanistic systems biology, with models of signaling
and regulatory processes involving Notch-Dll4, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF),
and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). These projects taught me how to translate
biological mechanisms into mathematical structures and how to use models to
generate experimentally relevant insight.

I subsequently expanded into quantitative systems pharmacology, oncology,
and virtual-population modeling. This work focuses on connecting drug
mechanisms and biological heterogeneity with clinically relevant outcomes.

I am now building additional expertise in pharmacometrics, including
noncompartmental analysis, population pharmacokinetics, covariate modeling,
model diagnostics, simulation, and uncertainty quantification.

## How I approach modeling

I am especially interested in models that are:

- mechanistically interpretable;
- informed by experimental or clinical data;
- transparent about uncertainty and limitations;
- evaluated for numerical and predictive robustness;
- designed to answer a clear scientific or therapeutic question.

For me, a model is most useful when it does more than reproduce observations:
it should clarify assumptions, connect evidence across scales, and help guide
the next scientific decision.

## Emerging directions

A long-term goal of my work is to apply quantitative pharmacology and systems
modeling to a broader range of therapeutic questions. I am particularly
interested in natural products, medicinal plants, and complex interventions
that are difficult to investigate using conventional single-target approaches.

This direction brings together my background in mechanistic modeling with
my growing experience in pharmacometrics and translational pharmacology.
